c.tagline: Cameroon's hilly capital, the city of seven hills.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow taxis run as shared cabs along fixed routes for a small flat fare; agree the price and whether you want it 'dépôt' (private) before getting in. Moto-taxis (called 'bend-skin') are common for short hops but riskier.

emergency.note: 117 reaches the police; 118 is the fire and ambulance service. Response times can be slow, so many residents and hotels arrange private clinic transport directly.

avoid.reason: Petty crime; caution at night. Anglophone NW/SW and Far North regions unsafe — check advisories

hood_desc: The leafy embassy quarter on the northern hills, home to most foreign diplomatic missions, expatriates, upscale restaurants and the city's nicest hotels; the safest, calmest and most convenient base for first-time visitors.
The administrative and commercial heart around Place du 20 Mai, the Reunification Monument and the Central Market; busy, walkable in patches and close to ministries, banks and the National Museum.
A dense, lively residential and nightlife pocket just north of downtown known for its bars, street food and small hotels; central and affordable but noisy after dark.
A green hillside district best known for the Mvog-Betsi Zoo-Botanical Park; quieter and more local, good for travelers who want parkland and everyday neighborhood life.

The traditional market district around the sprawling Mokolo market, one of the largest in the city; chaotic, authentic and cheap, suited to budget travelers who want to be in the thick of local commerce.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: Shared taxis and buses run roughly from dawn (around 5:30 AM) until mid-evening; after dark options thin out and moto-taxis or chartered cabs fill the gap.
transit.note: Yaoundé has no metro, tram or urban rail. Getting around means shared yellow taxis (the backbone of city transport), a limited network of city buses, and moto-taxis for short trips. Traffic is heavy on weekdays and much lighter at weekends.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver; there is no transit card or ticketing system. Carry small CFA-franc notes and coins as drivers rarely have change.

bus: Intercity coaches from the Nsam and Mvan terminals to Douala and other Cameroonian cities

Camrail overnight line north to N'Gaoundéré

Private/charter taxi to the city center (40-50 min)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for good service in nicer restaurants is appreciated.

food.name: Ndole
food.desc: Cameroon's national dish: bitterleaf boiled down with ground peanuts, crayfish and beef or shrimp, eaten with fried ripe plantain or miondo cassava sticks.

places.name: Chez Maman Africa
places.note: Home-style Cameroonian cooking; ndole, eru and koki made the way they are made at home.

places.name: Boukarou Lounge
places.note: Sit-down local kitchen popular with expats and Yaounde families alike.

places.name: Tchop & Yamo
places.note: Fast-service Cameroonian canteen, a cheap and dependable first taste of ndole.

food.name: Poulet DG
food.desc: Directeur General chicken - fried chicken pieces tossed with sweet plantain, carrot, green beans and tomato; a celebration dish now on every menu.

places.name: Boukarou Lounge
places.note: Often singled out locally for its poulet DG and its braised fish.

places.name: Maison Blanche
places.note: Long-running restaurant for grills and Cameroonian classics in generous portions.

places.name: Tchop & Yamo
places.note: Quick, affordable version if you want it without a long sit-down lunch.

food.name: Poisson braise
food.desc: Whole mackerel or tilapia scored, marinated in garlic, ginger and pepper, then charcoal-grilled and served with miondo, plantain and hot pepper sauce.

places.name: Maison Blanche
places.note: Known for grilled fish and seafood in a proper restaurant setting.

places.name: Grill stalls in Briqueterie
places.note: The city's best-known evening street-grill quarter; fish and soya skewers over charcoal.

places.name: Evening grills around Nlongkak
places.note: Roadside braziers fire up after dark; point at your fish and wait at a plastic table.

food.name: Koki
food.desc: Black-eyed peas ground to a paste with red palm oil and chilli, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed into a dense savoury pudding.

places.name: Chez Maman Africa
places.note: One of the few restaurants that cooks koki properly rather than only on request.

places.name: Marche du Mfoundi food stalls
places.note: Market cooks steam koki in leaf parcels each morning; cheapest and most authentic.

places.name: Marche Mokolo food stalls
places.note: Huge market with a whole aisle of cooked-food sellers doing koki and steamed plantain.

food.name: Eru with water fufu
food.desc: Anglophone Cameroon's favourite: shredded eru leaf and waterleaf stewed with palm oil, crayfish and tripe, mopped up with soft fermented cassava fufu.

places.name: Chez Maman Africa
places.note: Cooked to the standard of the Southwest, not a watered-down version.

places.name: Boukarou Lounge
places.note: Reliable eru alongside the rest of the Cameroonian canon.

places.name: Marche Mokolo food stalls
places.note: Market canteens serve eru with fufu at lunchtime for a few hundred francs.

food.name: Beignets-haricots-bouillie
food.desc: The classic Cameroonian breakfast trio - puffy fried dough balls, slow-stewed beans in palm oil, and sweet spiced corn or millet porridge.

places.name: Morning stalls in Briqueterie
places.note: Pavement fryers start before dawn; the standard workers' breakfast in Yaounde.

places.name: Tchop & Yamo
places.note: Serves beignets and beans all day if you miss the street vendors' morning window.

places.name: Marche du Mfoundi food stalls
places.note: Beignet women set up at the market gates alongside the porridge sellers.

food.name: Jus naturels (bissap and ginger)
food.desc: Chilled homemade juices - deep red hibiscus bissap, fiery ginger, tamarind and folere - sold in bottles and served with every local meal.

places.name: Tchop & Yamo
places.note: Fresh house juices are a menu fixture alongside the beans and beignets.

places.name: Chez Maman Africa
places.note: Bissap and ginger poured by the jug to go with the heavier stews.

places.name: Marche du Mfoundi vendors
places.note: Bottled bissap and ginger sold ice-cold from coolers around the market.

food.name: Matango (palm wine)
food.desc: Milky, lightly fermented sap tapped from raffia palms, drunk fresh and mildly sweet in the morning, sharper and stronger by evening.

places.name: Palm-wine bars in Briqueterie
places.note: Informal bars around the grill quarter serve matango by the calabash or bottle.

places.name: Boukarou Lounge
places.note: Easier setting to try it, plus local 33 Export and Mutzig beers.

places.name: Marche Mokolo drink stalls
places.note: Tappers bring in fresh matango from the villages most mornings.

landmarks: Notre-Dame des Victoires Cathedral
Yaoundé's bold triangular cathedral rises beside the central market, its sweeping modernist lines and Sunday choirs emblematic of the capital's spirit.
National Museum of Cameroon
Housed in the elegant former presidential palace, its galleries unpack Cameroon's 250 ethnic cultures through masks, thrones and royal regalia.
Reunification Monument
A spiraling concrete tower and statue commemorating the 1961 union of French and British Cameroons, the city's most recognizable modern symbol.
Mont Fébé
The forested mountain guarding the city's northern edge offers cooler air, a golf course and sweeping viewpoints over Yaoundé's seven hills.
Benedictine Monastery Museum of Mont Fébé
A hillside monastery whose small museum guards a superb collection of traditional Cameroonian art, from Bamileke masks to beaded thrones.
Basilique Marie-Reine-des-Apôtres (Mvolyé)
A grand hilltop basilica on the site of Cameroon's first Catholic mission, its soaring nave drawing pilgrims and panoramic photographers alike.
Mvog-Betsi Zoo
A conservation-minded zoo run with a British charity, sheltering rescued gorillas, mandrills and lions in the heart of the capital.
Mefou National Park
An easy day trip to Ape Action Africa's forest sanctuary, walking trails past rescued gorillas and chimpanzees in vast natural enclosures.
Marché Central
The capital's frenetic central market spills over several blocks with fabrics, produce and street food—an essential immersion in Yaoundé life.
Musée La Blackitude
A private museum curated by a traditional queen, displaying centuries-old royal artifacts, statuary and sacred objects from Cameroon's chiefdoms.

train.note: The Gare Voyageurs, just north of the city centre, is the hub of Camrail's network. New Intercity trains cover the Douala run in about 3 hours 45 minutes several times a day, and a nightly sleeper heads north to Ngaoundéré in roughly 15 hours, which is much the most comfortable way to reach northern Cameroon. Buy at the station a day or two ahead - online booking is unreliable - and watch your bags, as pickpockets and ticket touts work the platforms; older regional trains lack air conditioning and delays are routine. Cameroon has no cross-border passenger railway: the northern line ends at Ngaoundéré, from where travellers for Chad continue by road.

bus.note: Yaoundé's coach agencies are grouped into five terminals by direction - Mvan for Douala, the south and the east, Biyem-Assi for the west and northwest, plus Nsam, Tongolo and Mimboman - so make sure you go to the right one. Général Express Voyages, Finexs Voyages, Touristique Express and Buca Voyages are among the better-known carriers; it is worth paying extra for the 'prestige' or VIP classes, which have better-maintained vehicles and seatbelts, and the congested, checkpoint-heavy Douala road (about 4 hours) is best avoided at night. Tickets are sold at the agency counters and buses often leave only when full. No operator sells a through ticket across a border: for Gabon or Equatorial Guinea take a coach to Ambam or Kye-Ossi and change into a shared taxi at the frontier, and for Nigeria travel via Bamenda and the Ekok-Mfum crossing.

ferry.note: Yaoundé lies more than 200 km inland on a plateau and has no port or river service of any kind. The nearest passenger boats are on the coast at Douala and Limbe, including irregular speedboat crossings towards Calabar in Nigeria and Bioko in Equatorial Guinea, and those have to be arranged locally rather than booked in advance.

half.name: Mbalmayo
half.blurb: Timber and market town on the Nyong River, once a river port for forest products south of Yaoundé.

half.name: Obala
half.blurb: Farming town north of Yaoundé known for its produce market and surrounding cocoa plantations.

full.name: Kribi
full.blurb: Atlantic beach town where the Lobé Falls drop directly into the ocean, a popular weekend escape from the capital.
